overall_summary: Analysis of the deduplicated performance data reveals clear viewer preference for high-concept space and astrophysics 'What If' scenarios and extreme planetary extremes. Videos featuring immersive hypothetical framing ('What If You Fell Into...') and rare cosmic phenomena (such as liquid diamond planets, dark planets, and unusual planetary rain) drive significantly higher views and engagement (likes/comments-per-view) compared to older neurological facts or static historical trivia. Recent 7-day performance indicates strong sustained momentum for existential space concepts.

winning_patterns.evidence: Videos like 'What If You Fell Into a Liquid Diamond Planet?' (1,029 views, 38 likes) and 'What If You Fell Into the Planet of Burning Ice?' (972 views, 18 likes) outperform standard static space facts.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on hypothetical second-person survival and exploration scenarios applied to extreme celestial bodies.

winning_patterns.evidence: Titles detailing extreme planetary conditions such as 'The Planet Darker Than Coal: TrES-2b' (1,030 views) and 'This Planet Rains Supersonic Rubies!' (725 views) capture immediate attention.
winning_patterns.action: Produce more deep-dives into newly discovered exoplanets featuring impossible meteorological or physical laws.

weak_patterns.evidence: Videos focusing on internal psychological tricks or memory facts like 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' (5-53 views across iterations) show stagnant or negligible view velocities.
weak_patterns.action: Deprioritize standard psychological quick-facts unless framed as high-stakes dystopian mysteries or thriller-style micro-stories.

weak_patterns.evidence: Basic animal biology facts without a high-concept existential threat or bizarre anomaly (e.g., standard octopus or jellyfish facts) fail to break out past baseline views.
weak_patterns.action: Pivot animal content strictly toward cinematic survival, deep-sea abyss horrors, or prehistoric evolutionary oddities.
